_about: Guidance shown on action cards. Every entry must cite at least one source the team has opened. Entries without a source are ignored by the loader. These texts are conservative prototype wording, not medical orders; flight medicine staff would replace them with mission procedures.
criticalStep: Call your Crew Medical Officer now.
genericSteps: Review the result with your Crew Medical Officer.

entries.why: Blood sugar below 70 mg/dL is considered low.
steps: If it is still low, or you feel shaky, sweaty or confused, follow the 15-15 rule: 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, then re-check after 15 minutes.
Repeat until you are back in range, then eat a snack with protein and carbohydrate.

sources.label: CDC: Treatment of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)

entries.why: Potassium is important to heart and muscle function.
steps: Tell your Crew Medical Officer today.
Write down any symptoms you notice in your log.

entries.why: Potassium is important to heart function. A damaged (hemolyzed) sample can falsely raise potassium.
steps: Ask for a new sample if the draw was difficult: a damaged sample can falsely raise potassium.
Tell your Crew Medical Officer today.

sources.label: UHNM Pathology: Common problems affecting blood test results

entries.why: Low sodium can cause weakness, fatigue and confusion.
steps: Report weakness, fatigue or confusion right away.

entries.why: High sodium can be a sign of dehydration.
steps: Review your fluid intake with your Crew Medical Officer.

entries.why: Urea nitrogen is a waste product filtered by the kidneys; a high value can reflect dehydration.
steps: Review your fluid intake with your Crew Medical Officer.
Repeat at the next scheduled draw.

entries.why: AST is found in the liver and also in muscle; heavy muscle use can raise it.
steps: Log any intense exercise in the 24 hours before the draw.
Repeat at the next scheduled draw; tell your Crew Medical Officer if it stays high.

sources.label: Mayo Clinic content via Altru: AST blood test

entries.why: When blood waits too long before the serum is separated, glucose falls and potassium rises inside the tube.
steps: Do not act on this value alone. Repeat the measurement with a fresh sample.
Tell your Crew Medical Officer that several crew members show the same change.
